10.label: HOOK
10.trigger: It is to figure out three things: What from my experience actually works here? What do I need to learn about this new context? And what can I begin to prove here?

10.label: WHY THIS FEELS STRANGE WHEN YOU ARE EXPERIENCED
10.trigger: You can be experienced and still be new to the context. Those two things can be true at the same time. That is why I would not spend the first 90 days trying to prove that everything you already know works here. I would spend them finding the boundary between what you brought with you and what this environment still has to teach you.

10.label: 1 | READ
10.trigger: During READ, pay attention to four things: What is this team actually responsible for? Where do the important decisions sit? What does success mean here? And what do people around me know that was never written in the job description? A job description can tell you the formal job. The first few weeks start showing you the real one.

10.label: 1 | READ
10.trigger: During READ, pay attention to four things: What is this team actually responsible for? Where do the important decisions sit? What does success mean here? And what do people around me know that was never written in the job description? A job description can tell you the formal job. The first few weeks start showing you the real one.

10.label: WHAT READ DOES NOT MEAN
10.trigger: There is a difference between saying, “At my old company, we did it this way,” and saying, “I have seen a similar problem before. Can you help me understand what makes it different here?” The second sentence brings your experience into the room without assuming the room is the same.

10.label: THE CONVERSATION I WOULD HAVE
10.trigger: Ask something more useful: “What have you seen me pick up quickly?” “Where do I still need more context?” “Is there anything I am treating like my old environment that works differently here?”

10.label: THE CONVERSATION I WOULD HAVE
10.trigger: And ask: “What would you want to trust me with by the end of my first 90 days that you would not have trusted me with on day one?” That question turns the first 90 days into development, not performance theater.

10.label: 3 | PROVE
10.trigger: So I would use a different question: What can I prove here by day 90 that I could not prove on day one?

10.label: WHAT PROOF SHOULD SOUND LIKE
10.trigger: By the end of the first 90 days, I would want you to be able to finish a few sentences. “I came in assuming X. I learned Y.” “The part of my previous experience that helped most was X.” “The part I had to relearn was Y.”

10.label: STORY LOOP
10.trigger: There is a reversal I want you to remember: during your first 90 days, they are not the only ones evaluating. You are collecting evidence about the job too. We will come back to that after READ, TEST, and PROVE.

10.label: THE REVERSAL | THEY ARE NOT THE ONLY ONES EVALUATING
10.trigger: There is one more part of the first 90 days I want to add. They are not the only ones evaluating. You are collecting evidence too. Is this actually the job you accepted? Does the authority match what you were told? Are you getting access to the work you came here to do?

10.label: THE REVERSAL | THEY ARE NOT THE ONLY ONES EVALUATING
10.trigger: That does not automatically mean leave. Roles change. Priorities change. Organizations have real constraints. But you should notice the difference.

10.label: THE FIRST-90-DAYS READ
10.trigger: So if I were building a first-90-days plan for an experienced professional, I would keep it this simple. READ. What do I understand now that I did not understand on day one? TEST. What from my previous experience works here, what needs translating, and what does not?

10.label: THE FIRST-90-DAYS READ
10.trigger: Read the context. Test what traveled. Build new proof. And read the role back.

10.label: WATCH NEXT
10.trigger: And if your first 90 days are showing you that the job you started is not the job you thought you accepted, that is a different problem. I made the next video for exactly that. Watch “What to Do When Your New Job Isn’t the Job You Accepted” next.

11.label: THE ROLE-DRIFT READ
11.trigger: COST. What is the difference doing to my capability, evidence, compensation, or life? CHOICE. What can I clarify, negotiate, test, or decide next? That is a role-drift read. It gives you something more useful than “I hate this job” and something more honest than “I should just give it more time.”

11.label: 1 | EXPECTED
11.trigger: Write down the parts that mattered to your decision. Scope. Authority. Reporting line. Location. Travel. Compensation. Team. The kind of work you expected to spend meaningful time doing.

11.label: 2 | ACTUAL
11.trigger: And sometimes the actual role is narrower. You were hired for strategy and spend most of your time coordinating. You expected to lead a team and the team never arrived. You were told a decision was yours and discover that you can only recommend.

11.label: 2 | ACTUAL
11.trigger: The question is not, “Is this exactly what was written?” The better question is, “Is the job I am doing still close enough to the job I agreed to build my life and career around?”

11.label: 3 | COST
11.trigger: Imagine you expected a strategic role, but the first month is unusually operational because a launch is underway. That may be temporary. Now imagine six months later the strategic work still has not appeared, you are still doing work you already knew how to do, and there is no credible path to the scope you accepted.

11.label: THE FOUR COST LENSES
11.trigger: I would look at four costs. CAPABILITY. Is this role building judgment, scope, and experience you want to carry forward? EVIDENCE. Will you be able to prove meaningful work from this version of the job?

11.label: 4 | CHOICE
11.trigger: I would say something like: “When we discussed this role, I expected X. In practice, I am seeing Y. Is that temporary, or is this the role as it now exists?” That question gives the other person room to explain what changed without requiring you to pretend the difference is not real.

11.label: WHAT NOT TO DO
11.trigger: I would avoid two extremes. Do not convince yourself that every mismatch is a betrayal. A job can change for legitimate reasons.

11.label: THE ROLE-DRIFT READ
11.trigger: So put the four lines next to each other. EXPECTED. What did I reasonably believe I was accepting? ACTUAL. What is true now, based on the recurring pattern?

11.label: THE BOUNDARY
11.trigger: This framework does not tell you whether to leave. Sometimes the right choice is to stay because the drift is temporary or the actual role is better than the expected one. Sometimes you stay because leaving is not practical yet.

11.label: THE BOUNDARY
11.trigger: And sometimes the gap is large enough that you need to plan an exit. Your constraints are real. Compensation, health, caregiving, immigration, geography, timing, the market, and financial runway can all shape what is possible. The goal is not to force a dramatic decision. It is to make the decision from the job that actually exists.

11.label: CLOSE
11.trigger: The job description got you into the role. The first few months tell you what the role really is. If those two versions are different, name the difference before you normalize it.

11.label: WATCH NEXT
11.trigger: And if the role is depending on you more and more without building anything new in you, watch “If Your Company Needs You but Won’t Grow You” next.
